name: Fair
description: Some company is going to hold a fair in Byteland. There are $$$n$$$ towns in Byteland and $$$m$$$ two-way roads between towns. Of course, you can reach any town from any other town using roads. There are $$$k$$$ types of goods produced in Byteland and every town produces only one type. To hold a fair you have to bring at least $$$s$$$ different types of goods. It costs $$$d(u,v)$$$ coins to bring goods from town $$$u$$$ to town $$$v$$$ where $$$d(u,v)$$$ is the length of the shortest path from $$$u$$$ to $$$v$$$. Length of a path is the number of roads in this path. The organizers will cover all travel expenses but they can choose the towns to bring goods from. Now they want to calculate minimum expenses to hold a fair in each of $$$n$$$ towns.
input_specification: There are $$$4$$$ integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, $$$k$$$, $$$s$$$ in the first line of input ($$$1 \le n \le 10^{5}$$$, $$$0 \le m \le 10^{5}$$$, $$$1 \le s \le k \le min(n, 100)$$$) — the number of towns, the number of roads, the number of different types of goods, the number of different types of goods necessary to hold a fair. In the next line there are $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_{i} \le k$$$), where $$$a_i$$$ is the type of goods produced in the $$$i$$$-th town. It is guaranteed that all integers between $$$1$$$ and $$$k$$$ occur at least once among integers $$$a_{i}$$$. In the next $$$m$$$ lines roads are described. Each road is described by two integers $$$u$$$ $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$, $$$u \ne v$$$) — the towns connected by this road. It is guaranteed that there is no more than one road between every two towns. It is guaranteed that you can go from any town to any other town via roads.
output_specification: Print $$$n$$$ numbers, the $$$i$$$-th of them is the minimum number of coins you need to spend on travel expenses to hold a fair in town $$$i$$$. Separate numbers with spaces.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 986A — Fair [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
